summary: Long-duration space missions to the Moon and Mars expose astronauts to physiological and psychological hazards, compounded by communication delays with Earth. That's why we present ORBIT (Onboard Risk & Behavioral Insight Tracker), an autonomous cyber-physical system designed for continuous health and behavioral monitoring. ORBIT integrates a network of smart wearables—a vest, a wristband, and a headband—equipped with ESP32 microcontrollers and biometric sensors, communicating via the integrated ESP bluetooth capabilities in a closed network. The system employs a dual-layer artificial intelligence architecture: a lightweight Qwen model on the astronaut's edge device processes real-time vital signs and manages gamified cognitive tasks, while a heavier Qwen AI model on the Mission Control Dashboard performs predictive analytics, handles SOS alerts, and generates personalized health protocols. By combining physiological telemetry with behavioral insights, ORBIT mitigates the risks of isolation and physiological drift, enhancing crew autonomy and medical safety in extreme environments.
details:
ORBIT operates as a dual-layer ecosystem that monitors, predicts, and reacts to astronaut health. Physically, it consists of three smart garments: a vest (ECG, respiration, temperature, IMU), a wristband (heart rate, IMU), and a headband (camera, screen). These garments are powered by ESP32 microcontrollers that transmit physiological data to a local mobile device.


The software operates on two levels:

Edge Level (Astronaut): A lightweight Qwen AI model runs locally on the wrist device. It monitors vital signs, detects immediate SOS anomalies, and interacts with the astronaut through a gamified interface.

Mission Control Level (Dashboard): A heavy AI model on a local computer receives data from the entire crew. It analyzes long-term trends, predicts health risks (like fatigue or cardiovascular drift), provides visualizations of the crew, and generates personalized physical/mental work protocols.

Benefits
ORBIT provides real-time, autonomous health monitoring that does not rely on Earth-based communication, drastically reducing response times to medical emergencies. It combats the psychological toll of isolation through gamification. Furthermore, the system seamlessly bridges the gap between daily physical activity and long-term medical diagnosis, ensuring astronauts remain mission-ready.


Tools

Hardware: ESP32 microcontrollers, IMU sensors, ECG electrodes, thermistors, optical heart rate sensors, and an Android/iOS mobile device.

Software / AI: We utilized the Qwen lightweight Large Language Model for edge computing, paired with a heavy machine learning model (for predictive analytics and anomaly detection) on the dashboard.


Our project is highly creative because we merged clinical health monitoring with behavioral gamification. Instead of just displaying raw numbers, ORBIT tracks the astronaut's cognitive and physical health through mini-games (testing reflexes and communication) and a "Strava-like" leaderboard system. This unique approach uses behavioral data as a vital sign, turning health monitoring into an engaging, mission-oriented experience. Additionally, the system's dual-AI architecture—an on-body copilot and a mission-control brain—creates a completely autonomous ecosystem.

Considerations
We carefully considered the physical and technical constraints of spaceflight.

Sensor limitations: We recognized that invasive or complex metrics like glucose and EEG are difficult to measure non-invasively. For muscle/bone density loss, we designed the system to "prescribe" high-resolution scans (MRI/Tomography) within the spacecraft via the dashboard protocol.

Connectivity: We factored in the limited range of ESP bluetooth and mitigated it by planning to integrate LoRa repeaters.

Radiation: We incorporated a dedicated MOSFET radiation sensor to monitor cumulative exposure.

Psychological factors: We heavily considered the behavioral risks of confinement, ensuring our UI reduces stress rather than adding to it.
